Forgotten figures

The Matilda effect: when someone else gets the credit

Many women scientists have been denied credit for their discoveries. A historian gave it a name in 1993.

In 1993, the historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term Matilda effect to describe how women scientists' achievements are credited to male colleagues or forgotten. She took the name from Matilda Joslyn Gage, an American suffragist who as early as 1870 had denounced the way women inventors were ignored.

Some examples

Nettie Stevens discovered in 1905 that sex is determined by the X and Y chromosomes, but for years the credit went to Edmund Wilson. Rosalind Franklin obtained the key image for discovering the structure of DNA and was not properly acknowledged. Lise Meitner took part in discovering nuclear fission, and the Nobel went to Otto Hahn alone.

Psychology has its own cases: Mary Whiton Calkins completed a doctorate at Harvard that was never awarded to her because she was a woman. Recent studies show the effect persists in citations, prizes and authorship, though it is declining.

References

  1. Rossiter, M. W. (1993). The Matthew Matilda effect in science. Social Studies of Science, 23(2), 325–341.
  2. Ross, M. B. et al. (2022). Women are credited less in science than men. Nature, 608, 135–145.
